clue.text: Building site made over in the North-west

definitions.note: a phrase locating the place, not a noun

indicators.note: building means putting together into a new structure
made over means remade, so the letters are turned into something new

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A construction site in north-west England has been redeveloped.
explanation.walkthrough: Tameside is a borough of Greater Manchester, in England's North West.
explanation.definitionFit: Tameside is a metropolitan borough east of Manchester, which lies in the North West region of England.

clue.text: A flavouring that's quite new

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the herb used to flavour sauces and sweets
second meaning: in perfect unused condition

explanation.surface: A novel flavour on the market.
explanation.definitionFit: The herb is a common flavouring, and 'in mint condition' means as good as new.

clue.text: Many fish and swing for it!

definitions.note: a verb phrase meaning be hanged

parts.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals, a large number
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: A threat to the poacher who catches lots of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' looks like a noun; it is the verb. Using a Roman numeral for 'many' is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To swing for a crime is to be hanged, and a hanged body hangs loosely, swaying.

clue.text: Giving support to a collaborator as allowed

parts.note: a leg supports a table or chair
an ally works with you

explanation.surface: Helping a partner in crime, within the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Legally means in a manner permitted by law, the adverb matching 'as allowed'.

clue.text: One showing a preference for the Spanish in part

indicators.note: in places the words before it inside the word after it

parts.note: a sector is a part or division
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Someone partly drawn to things Spanish.
explanation.definitionFit: A selector picks one thing over another, as in the choosers of a sports team.

clue.text: Notice of government official's conduct

parts.note: an ad is a public notice
a minister heads a government department

explanation.surface: A report on how a minister has behaved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conduct' reads as the noun behaviour; it is the verb, to manage or run.
explanation.definitionFit: To administer something is to manage or run it, as you conduct business.

clue.text: May hold a clergyman up, being hollow

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it inside you

parts.note: may and can both mean be permitted to

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters run bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend

explanation.surface: May might lift up a vicar, who feels empty inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' poses as a name or the month; it is the verb meaning be allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavern is a large cave, a hollow in rock.

clue.text: Fence taking friend aside maybe

indicators.note: 'maybe' says the following word is only one possible arrangement of its letters

parts.note: a pal is a friend
the letters of this word, rearranged

explanation.surface: A fence takes a friend aside, perhaps to discuss stolen goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fence' tempts you toward the receiver of stolen goods, but here it is the barrier of stakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A palisade is a defensive barrier of pointed wooden stakes, a kind of fence.

clue.text: To win requires close attention

definitions.note: an infinitive standing for a verb

parts.note: a close is an end
to give ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: Winning demands concentration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close attention' reads as one phrase; split it into the noun close and the noun attention.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear yourself is to win someone's affection, so endear means win over.

clue.text: Animals in quarantine — a temporary measure

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow, tucked within their run of letters

parts.note: the tail of the first word, the lone article and the head of the next word run together; the rest is surrounding surface

explanation.surface: Keeping animals in quarantine is only a stopgap, a short-term precaution against disease.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the dash and read quaranti-NE A T-emporary straight through; the rest of the phrase is scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat is an old word for cattle, still used in crosswords and in 'neatsfoot oil', so it stands for farm animals.

clue.text: Quiet bars on the French coast

definitions.note: a phrase locating the place, not a noun

parts.note: grave in the sense of sober and subdued
bars as stripes or lines

explanation.surface: Peaceful pubs along the coast of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests drinking places; it means lines or stripes.
explanation.definitionFit: Gravelines is a port town on the Channel coast of northern France, near Dunkirk.

clue.text: A girl in some confusion

indicators.note: confusion jumbles things up, so the words beside it are scrambled

parts.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A young woman is somewhat flustered.
explanation.definitionFit: Simone is a female first name, and crosswords freely clue girls' names as 'a girl'.

clue.text: Personal service for which the pay's too uncertain

indicators.note: uncertain means unsettled, so the letters before it have no fixed order

parts.note: the ten letters to be rearranged, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A one-to-one job whose wages are too unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: Osteopathy is a hands-on therapy treating each patient's bones and joints individually.

clue.text: Foreigners left at six with the answer

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
taken as written
six in Roman numerals
ANS is the usual abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Visitors from abroad departed at six o'clock, taking the solution with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Latvians are people from Latvia, and to an Australian or British reader they are an example of foreigners.

clue.text: An upholder of the Christian word

definitions.text: An upholder of the Christian word

parts.words: An upholder of the Christian word
parts.note: surface reading: a defender of the faith or of Christian teaching
setter's reading: something that physically holds up the Bible in church

explanation.walkthrough: 'Upholder' sounds like a champion of doctrine, but taken literally it is a stand that holds up the book.
explanation.definitionFit: A lectern is the reading stand in a church on which the Bible rests, literally holding up the scripture.

clue.text: The guy going to the dogs?

definitions.text: The guy going to the dogs?

parts.words: The guy going to the dogs?
parts.note: surface reading: a man falling into ruin
setter's reading: literally attending greyhound racing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going to the dogs' is an idiom for decline; the question mark asks you to take it literally, as a night at the greyhound track.
explanation.definitionFit: A racegoer attends race meetings, and the dogs is everyday slang for greyhound racing.

clue.text: Changeable — change operant

indicators.note: an instruction to change the following word, here by moving its letters around

parts.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A note that something variable has had its operating behaviour altered.
explanation.definitionFit: Protean comes from Proteus, the sea god who kept altering his shape, so it means variable.

clue.text: 7 down could present a martial appearance

indicators.note: could present suggests the following letters may be shown in another form
an appearance is an outward form, here a new form of the words before it

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cave might give a warlike impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 down is CAVERN. 'Martial' sounds like the point of the clue, but it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Altamira is the famous cave in northern Spain with prehistoric paintings, an example of a cavern.

clue.text: Sporting but tiresome

definitions.meaning: first meaning: having on, as in sporting a hat

explanation.surface: Games are fun but exhausting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' suggests athletics; it means showing off clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To be wearing a badge is to sport it, and a wearing day is one that tires you out.

clue.text: An unmarried person

parts.note: surface reading: someone who never married, a bachelor or spinster
setter's reading: someone whose marriage has been undone by law

explanation.walkthrough: Bachelor and spinster both fit eight letters, but the crossing letters point to someone who was married and no longer is.
explanation.definitionFit: A divorcee was once wed and is now legally single, so is unmarried in the undone sense.

clue.text: Old Greek having one over — a single article

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
on top of something is over it
a single is one, the Roman numeral I
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek with one item too many.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ionians were one of the main peoples of ancient Greece, settled around the Aegean.

clue.text: Blunders made by a seaman the engineers backed

indicators.note: backed means moved backwards, so the whole run of letters before it is read from the end

parts.note: taken as written
a tar is a sailor
RE, the Royal Engineers of the British Army

explanation.surface: Mistakes caused by a sailor whom the engineers supported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' looks like 'supported'; it turns the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are listed errors in a printed work, so a plural noun for mistakes.

clue.text: Enriches work in every way

indicators.note: in places the word before it inside the letters that follow

parts.note: the four compass points, every direction you can go
to do is to work

explanation.surface: Labour makes one richer in all respects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' means a direction here, and every direction gives the compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow is to provide with money or qualities, so it means enrich.

clue.text: Finish up very annoyed when put at risk

parts.note: to finish up is to end
made very cross

explanation.surface: Someone ends up furious once they are placed in danger.
explanation.definitionFit: Endangered describes something exposed to danger or threatened, the past participle matching 'put'.

clue.text: Swindle involving a painter and politician

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A fraud that implicates an artist and a member of parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: A ramp is British slang for a racket or swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a ramp is a dishonest scheme for profit, such as overcharging.

clue.text: Agitation occasioned by for example a right turn

indicators.note: a turn sends things round the other way, so the run of letters before it is read backwards

parts.note: e.g., for example
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Distress caused when a driver turns right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right turn' reads as a driving manoeuvre; 'turn' is the instruction to reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Rage is violent anger, an extreme state of agitation.

clue.text: A club graduates hasten to join

parts.note: Masters of Arts
hie is an old word for hurry

explanation.surface: Graduates rush to become members of a society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A club' looks like a society to join; it is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A mashie is an old name for a golf iron, roughly the modern five-iron.

clue.text: She makes daily deliveries

parts.note: surface reading: a woman who delivers every day, perhaps a midwife or milkwoman
setter's reading: dailies are daily papers, which she delivers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' points at a midwife, but a daily here is a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsgirl delivers the newspapers, the dailies, to homes each morning.
